introduction: Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá wrote to people who knew Ḥáfiẓ, Sa‘dí and Rúmí by heart, and they quote them as Paul quoted Aratus to the Athenians: a line everyone knows, turned to a new purpose. This guide gathers such quotations with ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s remarks on poetry itself: verse reaches further than prose, its purpose is to disclose inner mysteries, and praise without meaning is “glass without a lamp”. The imagery is that of the Persian lyric: the tress, the wine-cup, the nightingale and the rose, Joseph’s shirt. The Song of Songs is the nearest thing in the Bible. Aristotle and Shelley defend poetry’s seriousness; the Qur’an and Plato distrust poets; FitzGerald’s Omar shows what happens to this imagery when its key is lost.
questions: Why would a religious teacher quote love poetry and wine poetry? What does reading 8 say verse is for?
The Qur’an says the erring follow the poets. How do the readings decide which poets to follow?
Choose one quoted couplet. What does it say that a plain sentence could not?
Several lines are repeated to different people. What does a line gain by being a common possession?
How do you tell when wine means wine?

outside.why: Rapture raining from the clouds above. The Bible’s own love poem: many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.
The most pleasant city is where the beloved lives. Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.
The name was mentioned, and hearer and speaker began to dance. Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard are sweeter.
A lover speaking without lips. Hearken to the reed-flute, how it complains, lamenting its banishment from its home.
Verse is more pleasant than prose and its influence greater. Aristotle: poetry is a more philosophical and a higher thing than history.
The purpose of poetry is to express the inner mysteries. Shelley: poets are the hierophants of an unapprehended inspiration, the mirrors of the gigantic shadows which futurity casts upon the present.

Odes that are words without meaning, glass without a lamp. The Qur’an’s verdict was general: as for poets, the erring follow them. The readings quote poets on almost every page. What distinguishes the verse they praise from the verse the Qur’an distrusts?
Socrates: poets say many fine things, but do not understand the meaning of them.
An ode in praise of the Prophet made its poet renowned. Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise.
Prophets have had their poets. Paul at Athens quoted the Greeks’ own: as certain also of your own poets have said, for we are also his offspring.
Now spring has come and the nightingale begins. The winter is past, the flowers appear on the earth; the time of the singing of birds is come.
The Shaykh went about the city with a lamp, weary of beasts, seeking a human being. Rúmí’s lines retell the Greek story: Diogenes lit a lamp in broad daylight and said, I am looking for a man.
This reading is the Qur’anic verse the poets draw on: We offered the trust unto the heavens and the earth and the hills, but they shrank from bearing it, and man assumed it.
“Love’s fool am I.” The lunatic, the lover and the poet are of imagination all compact.
At dawn the Friend came to my bed. By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth.
No commotion in the city but the curl of the Beloved’s tress. As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters.

The wine-cup in one hand, the Beloved’s tress in the other. FitzGerald’s Omar: a jug of wine, a loaf of bread, and thou beside me singing in the wilderness. English readers took his wine literally. How do the readings want Ḥáfiẓ’s wine and tresses taken, and how can a reader tell?

“Drink wine in secret, for they accuse of infidelity.” Look not thou upon the wine when it is red: at the last it biteth like a serpent. A religion that forbids wine quotes its praises in verse. What does the image carry that plain speech could not?
The souls of the lions of God are united. Whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it.
The chain that bound the Joseph of the prison turns to mercy’s chain. Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.
I am drowning, so what fear have I of getting wet? Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.
Whoever is more favoured at this feast is given a fuller cup of tribulation. Whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth.
The tradition behind the couplet: which of the people is tried most severely? The Prophets, then those nearest to them.
These bitter days shall pass. Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
The reading quotes this passage itself: to every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.
Yesterday none was like you; today you are what none should be. The Lion and the Lizard keep the courts where Jamshyd gloried and drank deep.
False hawks have learned the falcon’s cry. Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing.
The herald bearing Joseph’s garment opens Jacob’s eyes. When he saw the wagons which Joseph had sent, the spirit of Jacob their father revived.
Firdawsí on the first king to found dominion. Shelley on what becomes of it: look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair! Nothing beside remains.

shortfall: The guide is itself an anthology of quoted verse, much of it repeated from letter to letter; companions were set where a new poem or theme enters, about one reading in three.
